Administer an initial loading dose of magnesium sulfate to treat eclampsia, followed by referral to a higher level of care. 3. Perform manual removal of the placenta when clinically indicated. 4. Advanced-level associate clinicians are recommended to perform vacuum extraction during childbirth and manual removal of the placenta. 5. Administer a maintenance dose of magnesium sulfate to prevent eclampsia, followed by referral to a higher level of care. 6. Administer a maintenance dose of magnesium sulfate to treat eclampsia, followed by referral to a higher level of care. 7. Perform cesarean sections when necessary, as recommended for non-specialist doctors with appropriate training and monitoring. 8. Conduct external cephalic version (ECV) for breech presentation at term, as recommended for non-specialist doctors with targeted monitoring and evaluation. 9. Many WHO Member States have implemented strategies to increase access to effective health interventions. One such approach is task shifting or task sharing, which involves training available health cadres to take on new responsibilities they were not previously trained for. This strategy aims to optimize the use of health system resources and improve health outcomes. 10. Task shifting can enhance health system performance by increasing access to specific interventions. It involves training non-specialist health workers to safely and effectively deliver interventions, thereby addressing gaps in healthcare access. 11. The WHO supports efforts to increase skilled birth attendance and improve intrapartum care, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). Task shifting strategies play a complementary role in achieving these goals and improving maternal and newborn health outcomes. 12. The global health workforce crisis significantly impacts the achievement of health-related Millennium Development Goals (MDGs). According to the 2006 World Health Report, 57 countries face chronic shortages of human resources in the health sector, with the majority being LMICs. 13. Sub-Saharan Africa, for example, bears 24% of the global disease burden but has only 3% of the global health workforce and accounts for just 1% of global health expenditure. In contrast, the Americas region, with 14% of the world’s population, has 37% of the global health workforce and accounts for 50% of global health expenditure. 14. Within-country inequalities in health workforce distribution are also common, particularly in low-income countries. For instance, only 24% of physicians and 38% of nurses work in rural areas, even though these regions house half of the world’s population. 15. The shortage of skilled birth attendants is a critical indicator of the global health workforce crisis. Approximately 60 million births occur annually outside health facilities, with 52 million of these lacking the support of a skilled birth attendant. 16. Countries with high neonatal and maternal mortality rates often have low levels of skilled birth attendance, few cesarean deliveries, and low physician density. Conversely, nations with low neonatal and maternal mortality rates typically have high levels of skilled birth attendance, more cesarean deliveries, and higher physician density. 17. Addressing gaps in health coverage and improving maternal and newborn health outcomes require active human resource policy interventions. Optimizing health worker roles through task shifting is a key strategy to achieve these objectives. 18. National health strategies should focus on improving access to quality care and increasing skilled birth attendance. Efforts to establish universal access to sexual and reproductive health and rights are also essential. 19. Lay health workers (LHWs) have been trained in some settings to deliver specific interventions, either independently or as part of community-based teams. LHWs are defined as individuals trained to perform health-related functions but without formal professional certification. 20. In some cases, traditional birth attendants (TBAs) have been recruited and trained to deliver individual interventions, such as promoting basic newborn care, as part of broader programs to improve access to care. 21. Professional cadres, such as auxiliary nurses and midwives, have also received additional training to perform tasks beyond their initial competencies, including minor surgical procedures. 22. In certain instances, new cadres, such as non-physician clinicians (NPCs), have been created to formally recognize those with advanced surgical competencies. 23. The WHO guidance aims to provide evidence-based recommendations to optimize the delivery of key maternal and newborn health interventions. These recommendations are intended for health policymakers, managers, and stakeholders at regional, national, and international levels. 24. The guidance emphasizes the importance of adapting and implementing recommendations based on the political and health system context of each country. 25. The WHO’s Knowledge-to-Action framework supports the development of evidence-based guidelines and their implementation. This process includes identifying critical questions, retrieving evidence, synthesizing and grading evidence, and formulating recommendations. 26. The guidance also highlights the need for targeted monitoring and evaluation to ensure the safe and effective delivery of interventions by relevant health worker categories. 27. The implementation of these recommendations depends on various political, financial, and health system factors, which are further discussed in the document. 28. The recommendations are compatible with other WHO-approved guidelines and aim to facilitate universal access to effective maternal and newborn health interventions.
